entries.title: What SMPL is
entries.answer: SMPL.ai is a Financial Intelligence platform built specifically for SaaS companies. We connect the systems finance already uses — accounting, CRM, HR, billing — standardize the data, calculate company-specific metrics, and generate executive reporting, forecasting, and AI-supported analysis with evidence behind every number. We sit above your systems of record; we do not replace your ERP.
entries.source: Executive Summary, 'What SMPL.ai is'

entries.title: Not a dashboard / BI tool
topics: how is this different from BI
isn't this just a BI tool
keywords: how is this different from bi
isn't this just a bi tool
entries.answer: It isn't a dashboard and it isn't a system of record. It's the decision-support layer that sits above the systems of record — the layer every SaaS finance team currently rebuilds by hand in spreadsheets every month. A BI tool lets you drill from a summary toward more granular numbers within one system; our lineage runs all the way to the original source record, whichever system it came from.
entries.source: Investor Overview + Technical Whitepaper, canonical data model

entries.title: What makes SMPL different
entries.answer: Three things, by design and not as features bolted on: consistent results — the same inputs always produce the same outputs; transparent by design — every conclusion traces to underlying evidence and uncertainty is flagged, not hidden; and institutional knowledge — we preserve how your organization defines and measures its business and reproduce any report exactly as it was originally delivered.
entries.source: Executive Summary, 'What makes SMPL.ai different'

entries.title: What is your moat
entries.answer: Our moat is the financial intelligence architecture — not AI alone. Individual AI features can be copied; a governed architecture that runs deterministic calculations first, preserves institutional memory of how each customer defines their business, and consistently produces trusted, explainable outputs is much harder to replicate. The durable advantage is architecture, methodology, and explainability together — governed financial intelligence, not a model feature.
entries.source: Meeting Copilot KB §6 'What is your moat?' / 'Is AI your advantage?' / 'What makes SMPL difficult to copy?'; §3 'Why is architecture your moat?'

entries.title: Adapts to your process
topics: do we have to change our process
how do you handle our ARR definition
keywords: do we have to change our process
how do you handle our arr definition
entries.answer: SMPL adapts to your finance organization instead of asking you to adapt to the software. You keep your definition of ARR, your forecasting methodology, and the board metrics your leadership already understands — the platform learns them once and automates them. Methodology is configuration the engine executes, not hardcoded logic, so the engine is the same for every customer but your configuration is yours.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Financial Intelligence Engine

entries.title: Deterministic calculations
entries.answer: Every calculation is deterministic: given the same inputs and methodology configuration, the engine returns the identical output on every run. The mechanism is versioning, not caching — each calculation runs against a specific timestamped snapshot. A report generated in March, reproduced today, reads exactly as it did in March, even if the underlying data was later corrected. Both the old and new views are correct; they answer 'what did we know then' versus 'what do we know now.'
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Deterministic Calculations

entries.title: Evidence and explainability
topics: can you back up the numbers
keywords: can you back up the numbers
entries.answer: Every number traces to the specific source records that produced it — an invoice, an opportunity, a GL entry — not just an intermediate total. Explanations are generated the same way: a statement like 'expansion ARR beat forecast by $420K, driven by three enterprise upsells that closed early' comes from those three actual opportunity records, not a template. If the data doesn't support a specific explanation, the platform says so rather than inventing a plausible-sounding one.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Explainability and Evidence

entries.title: Confidence signals on numbers
topics: what happens if confidence is low
keywords: what happens if confidence is low
entries.answer: Every number and explanation carries an explicit confidence signal. A value from complete, well-structured data reads high-confidence; a value derived by inference — say, ARR estimated from invoice history rather than an explicit contract record — reads visibly lower, with a note on what would resolve it. Confidence is never collapsed into false certainty in either direction. When confidence is low, the UI flags it and explanations stay conservative — we show what is known and what would raise confidence, rather than collapsing uncertainty into a fake-precise number.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Explainability and Evidence

entries.title: Period close governance
entries.answer: Each reporting period moves through an explicit close workflow. Once a period is finalized, corrections do not rewrite history — they are recorded as new dated entries that supersede the previous ones. That way you can always answer what the numbers were when leadership made a decision, versus what they are after a correction.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Governance

entries.title: Period close governance (internal deep)
entries.answer: Each reporting period moves through an explicit workflow: load, validate, lock, freeze, report. Once frozen, a period doesn't reopen — a correction is recorded as a new dated entry linked to the one it supersedes, producing a new snapshot going forward while the original stays intact. That's what makes 'what did we know, and when did we know it' an answerable question rather than an aspiration.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Governance (internal)

entries.title: vs Cube
topics: how do you compare to Cube
keywords: how do you compare to cube
entries.answer: Cube serves a similar buyer, and its AI messaging can sound like ours on paper. The difference is architectural: Cube centers on bi-directional Excel and Sheets sync — finance still builds and maintains the model in spreadsheets, and AI makes that faster. That architecture cannot guarantee deterministic calculations or board decks that reproduce exactly after a restatement the way our Financial Intelligence Engine does. We compete on governed SaaS financial intelligence — consistent results, evidence, and institutional methodology — not on making spreadsheet models smarter. If the objection is simply “why not Cube,” answer on architecture: spreadsheet-centric bi-directional sync versus a governed calculation engine with reproducible board outputs.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Competitive Landscape

entries.title: vs Power BI
entries.answer: Power BI is excellent at visualizing data you already trust. SMPL is the governed financial intelligence layer that produces those trusted SaaS numbers — ARR waterfalls, tie-outs, board packages — with deterministic calculations and evidence before any chart. Put simply: Power BI shows the picture; we produce the finance-grade outputs BI tools consume. Many customers still use Power BI or Excel for ad hoc views on top of SMPL.
entries.source: Meeting Copilot KB competitive rewrite; Investor Overview positioning

entries.title: vs Tableau
entries.answer: Tableau presents information beautifully. SMPL produces trusted financial outputs for SaaS finance — standardized metrics, evidence-backed variance, and board-ready packages — then explains them. Visualization tools assume the numbers are already correct; we are the layer that makes SaaS financial numbers correct, consistent, and explainable across systems.
entries.source: Meeting Copilot KB competitive rewrite

entries.title: vs Snowflake
entries.answer: Snowflake stores and serves data. SMPL turns operational and finance data into governed financial intelligence — SaaS metrics, statements, scenarios, and AI commentary grounded in engine outputs. A warehouse is optional for us: we can work with shares or exports when useful, but the product is the intelligence layer, not another place to park tables. Customers with Snowflake still need the finance methodology and explainability SMPL provides.
entries.source: Meeting Copilot KB competitive rewrite

entries.title: vs ChatGPT / general AI
entries.answer: ChatGPT is a general assistant without your governed financial context. SMPL calculates trusted SaaS metrics first with a deterministic engine, then uses AI only to explain those validated results with evidence. Paste a P&L into ChatGPT and you get fluent prose that can still be wrong on ARR, NRR, or restatements. We keep AI after the numbers — and never as the system of record or a GL writer.
entries.source: Meeting Copilot KB competitive rewrite

entries.title: vs Mosaic (FP&A)
topics: how do you compare to Mosaic
keywords: how do you compare to mosaic
entries.answer: Mosaic was a mid-market SaaS FP&A platform — SaaS metrics, planning, and reporting with ERP/CRM/HRIS integrations — and is now part of HiBob as Bob Finance rather than a standalone FP&A product. If someone is comparing us to Mosaic's old positioning, we compete on governed financial intelligence for SaaS: deterministic calculations, evidence behind numbers, and board-ready packages that sit above systems of record. We are not an HCM suite add-on; we are purpose-built for SaaS finance intelligence. Fair to evaluate Bob Finance if they are already deep in HiBob — different buying center and architecture.
entries.source: Public Mosaic/HiBob positioning; Investor Overview competitive framing

entries.title: vs Excel as the reporting engine
entries.answer: Excel remains great for ad hoc analysis — we are not trying to ban spreadsheets. What Excel should not be is the enterprise reporting engine that recreates ARR bridges, board packs, and restatements by hand every month. SMPL automates that repetitive, error-prone layer with deterministic calculations and institutional methodology, while finance still uses Excel where judgment and exploration matter.
entries.source: Meeting Copilot KB competitive rewrite

entries.title: vs QuickBooks / incumbents
entries.answer: Incumbent accounting platforms are shipping AI variance analysis and commentary, and they'll keep closing surface-level feature gaps. Our durable advantage isn't a feature checklist — it's a data architecture built natively for SaaS metrics like ARR waterfalls, NRR and GRR, and quota ramp curves, with determinism and evidence attached by design, not general-ledger AI bolted on after the fact.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Competitive Landscape

entries.title: vs Rillet
topics: how do you compare to Rillet
keywords: how do you compare to rillet
entries.answer: Rillet is not a head-to-head competitor in the usual sense — it replaces or modernizes the system of record / GL path, while SMPL is the financial intelligence layer that sits above Rillet or any other general ledger. We see a natural complementary partnership: they own books; we own governed SaaS metrics, evidence, and executive packages on top. If someone frames “why not Rillet,” clarify category first — ERP/GL versus intelligence — then show how we work together rather than rip-and-replace.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Competitive Landscape

entries.title: Target market / ICP
entries.answer: High-growth SaaS companies in roughly the $5 million to $50 million ARR range — the band where finance complexity first outpaces finance headcount, where companies first build a real FP&A function and first outgrow QuickBooks and spreadsheets at the same time. There are more than 27,000 SaaS companies in the US alone.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Market opportunity

entries.title: Market growth
entries.answer: Estimates of the FP&A software market range from roughly $5 to $9 billion today, and nearly all of them agree on the direction: double-digit growth driven by the shift from spreadsheet-based planning to AI-native platforms. MGI Research puts cloud FP&A at nearly $8.5 billion in 2026, growing 28 percent year over year.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Market opportunity

entries.title: Business impact / ROI
topics: how much time do you save
keywords: how much time do you save
entries.answer: Four things. Speed — reporting that takes weeks after close is done in minutes once data is loaded. Effort — a single ARR reporting package can consume 40 to 80 hours of finance time today, and we automate most of it. Confidence — every deliverable ships with the data behind it, reviewed before it's shared. Alignment — finance, leadership, and the board work from one trusted view instead of reconciling spreadsheets.
entries.source: Executive Summary, Business impact

entries.title: Business model
entries.answer: A subscription platform sold directly to finance leadership, with a land-and-expand motion: customers start with core financial reporting and close automation, then expand into GTM efficiency, workforce modeling, and scenario planning as trust builds. Go-to-market runs through direct outreach to CFOs and VPs of Finance, plus partnerships with modern accounting platforms and advisory firms that reach the same buyer warmer than cold outbound.
entries.source: Investor Overview, Business model

entries.title: Where we are / traction
entries.answer: Platform design is complete — every data connection, calculation, and control is fully specified — and we can demonstrate it today on realistic SaaS data. We're not yet live with paying customers, which is exactly why we're bringing in a small number of design partners first, to validate against real data and shape the roadmap ahead of general availability.
entries.source: Executive Summary / Investor Overview, Where we are

entries.title: Implementation timeline
entries.answer: Same deliverables either way — dashboards, ARR, statements, board/MD&A, commentary, methodology config, and validation. For early customers, about one week is realistic when access is ready and we apply existing templates and playbooks (configuration and proof, not inventing the system). Four to six weeks is what the calendar can look like when discovery is heavy: first-time source mapping, waiting on legal/IT/exports, messy data, or multiple validation loops. North star is hours-to-a-day as more source systems are documented and productized. Elapsed time is driven by template-vs-one-off work plus how fast the customer unblocks access. Browser SaaS — nothing to install.

entries.title: Data security and how customers can trust us
topics: how do we trust your security
why should we trust you with our data
keywords: how do we trust your security
why should we trust you with our data
entries.answer: On data security: architecture first. SMPL is browser SaaS that reads and reconciles your finance systems — it does not post back to your GL or ERP. Data is encrypted in transit with TLS and at rest in managed Postgres. Tenants are isolated by organization ID on every warehouse path, so Org A cannot read Org B. Access is invite-based magic-link login with role-based views. AI keys stay on the API; narrative is drafted from engine outputs, not invented numbers. We are pursuing SOC 2 Type I (Security, Availability, Confidentiality) — we do not claim a completed SOC 2 report today. For IT we share the architecture diagram, DPA, subprocessors, and questionnaire answers.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram + SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2 + Technical Whitepaper

Encrypted in transit (TLS) and at rest in managed Postgres; tenants isolated by organization ID
Invite-based magic-link login with role-based views; AI keys stay on the API; narrative from engine outputs
Pursuing SOC 2 Type I (Security, Availability, Confidentiality) — not claiming a completed SOC 2 report today
For IT: architecture diagram, DPA, subprocessors, and questionnaire answers

entries.title: Encryption in transit and at rest
entries.answer: Yes. Traffic to the application and API is protected with HTTPS/TLS in transit. Customer warehouse data is stored in managed Postgres with encryption at rest provided by the database platform. That is the baseline we document for IT questionnaires and security reviews.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram, Security Posture; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2

entries.title: Multi-tenant isolation
topics: can another customer see our data
keywords: can another customer see our data
entries.answer: The warehouse and API are multi-tenant by design. Customer data is scoped by organization ID, and API queries require that tenant context — Org A cannot read Org B's warehouse. That isolation model is what we document for security reviews and SOC 2 readiness evidence.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram; Architecture Master, Multi-tenancy; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2

do you post to the GL

entries.answer: No. SMPL reads and reconciles source systems — accounting/GL, CRM, billing, HRIS — and does not post journals or write back into your ERP or general ledger. Your systems of record stay systems of record; we are the intelligence layer above them.

entries.title: Hosting and deployment model
entries.answer: SMPL is a secure browser-based SaaS application — no customer-installed client and no infrastructure for your team to manage. End users access dashboards and exports through a modern browser. The standard deployment separates the web app, API services, and multi-tenant Postgres warehouse, with production and sandbox environments. We can share the IT technical diagram under NDA for architecture review.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram; Technical Whitepaper, Delivery

entries.title: System architecture overview
topics: tell me about your system architecture
keywords: tell me about your system architecture
entries.answer: SMPL is a browser-based SaaS app: Next.js on Vercel for the frontend, a FastAPI API on Railway, and Neon Postgres as a multi-tenant warehouse. We sit above your systems of record — we do not replace the ERP or GL. The financial engine runs deterministic calculations first; AI is used afterward for narrative over those grounded numbers. Happy to share the IT technical diagram under NDA for a deeper review.

entries.title: Named subprocessors (sales-internal)
entries.answer: Sales-internal named stack (confirm before customer-facing disclosure packs): frontend on Vercel (Next.js), API on Railway (FastAPI), warehouse/auth data on Neon Postgres, magic-link email via Resend, AI narrative via Anthropic Claude with OpenAI as fallback, billing via Stripe. Prefer the abstracted architecture language externally unless the prospect has the current subprocessors list / DPA exhibit. Update this list whenever vendors change.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2 §7–8

entries.title: Where customer data is stored
entries.answer: Customer financial warehouse data lives in our managed multi-tenant Postgres database, accessed only through the application and API with tenant scoping. The web app and API run on managed cloud hosts — not on customer laptops or on-prem servers. Exact region and the named vendor list are covered in the subprocessors / DPA materials we share for IT review; we do not invent residency guarantees that are not in those documents.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2, system boundary

entries.title: Authentication today (magic link)
entries.answer: Users sign in with an email magic link — Auth.js passwordless login delivered by email — then a JWT session with organization membership and plan entitlements. Access is invite-based: we provision the organization and invite seats; users are not inventing their own unmanaged accounts into a tenant. Seat limits apply per plan.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram, Authentication; CUSTOMER_ACCESS.md

entries.title: SSO roadmap (honest)
entries.answer: Today authentication is email magic-link with org membership. Enterprise SSO — SAML/OIDC — is on the roadmap as an option for buyers that need it; we do not claim SSO is generally available today. For design partners we can discuss timeline honestly against your IdP requirements rather than overpromise.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram, Authentication; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2 (SSO backlog)

entries.title: SOC 2 status (pursuing)
topics: do you have a SOC report
entries.answer: We are pursuing SOC 2 — readiness work is in progress — and we do not claim a completed SOC 2 certification or issued report today. Target path is Type I first, covering Security, Availability, and Confidentiality; Type II follows after an observation window. Until a report is issued, the honest language is 'pursuing' or 'in progress,' and we unblock IT with architecture, encryption, tenant isolation, no GL write-back, auth model, AI handling, DPA, and questionnaire answers.

entries.title: SOC 2 scope path (sales-internal)
entries.answer: Internal: default Type I scope is Security + Availability + Confidentiality. Processing Integrity is deferred by default — do not market PI as third-party proof that ARR math or the engine is 'certified correct.' Privacy criterion skipped for now. Prefer sales unblockers (DPA, subprocessors, security one-pager, architecture) while controls and evidence mature. Never imply an issued report before it exists.

entries.title: AI hallucinations / how we prevent them
entries.answer: Yes — generative AI can invent narrative if left unconstrained. We prevent that by grounding commentary in numbers the deterministic engine already calculated, keeping humans in the review loop for board-facing packages, and never letting AI invent ledger figures. Where the data does not support a claim, we fail closed rather than fabricate an explanation.

topics: what systems do you connect to
entries.answer: We ingest from the systems finance already uses: ERP/GL such as NetSuite, Rillet, or QuickBooks; CRM such as Salesforce or HubSpot; billing such as Stripe or Maxio; HRIS such as Rippling or Workday; plus treasury extracts as needed. Today that is via versioned CSV or white-glove load — for example Snowflake share, object storage, or SFTP — normalized into our canonical model for reporting. Scheduled native connectors into that same model are on the roadmap; we do not claim they are generally available today.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram, Data Sources; Architecture Master ingestion today vs future; Technical Whitepaper, Canonical Data Model

entries.title: Production and sandbox environments
entries.answer: Yes — we separate production and sandbox/staging environments for the app, API, and database so customer production data is not mixed with preview or staging work. That separation is part of how we describe change management and go-live hygiene to IT.
entries.source: IT Technical Diagram, Environments; SOC 2 Readiness Reference v2

entries.title: Platform features overview
entries.answer: SMPL is a SaaS financial intelligence layer — not a BI dashboard and not an ERP. In the product you get executive dashboards, ARR/MRR waterfalls, the three financial statements with tie-outs, Actual vs Budget vs Forecast scenarios, pipeline and GTM views, board PowerPoint and MD&A-style Excel packages, and AI-assisted executive commentary grounded in the same numbers. Higher plans unlock Management P&L, workforce, and cash forecast modules. We sit above your GL, CRM, billing, and HR systems and do not post back to them.

entries.title: SEO / meta tags (marketing site)
entries.answer: SEO and meta tags are a marketing-site concern, not a product feature in customer meetings. Title, description, Open Graph, and structured data live on smpl-ai.com pages and are monitored in Google Search Console — they are not something configured inside the SMPL app for a prospect tenant. If someone is asking about discoverability of our public site, point them to the live marketing pages; if they mean product analytics SEO, that is out of scope for a finance intelligence demo.
entries.source: Marketing site / Search Console note for Sales Talk Track

entries.title: ARR / MRR waterfall reporting
entries.answer: Yes — ARR and MRR are first-class. You get a roll-forward waterfall: beginning, new, expansion, contraction, churn, reactivation where modeled, and ending — with drilldown to the underlying movements. Retention concepts like NRR and GRR are part of the SaaS finance model, not bolt-on spreadsheet formulas. How you define ARR is configured for your org rather than forced into a generic template.
entries.source: Reporting Logic MRR/ARR; Technical Whitepaper native SaaS primitives; company context §3

entries.title: Three financial statements
topics: income statement balance sheet cash flow
entries.answer: Yes — income statement (P&L), balance sheet, and cash flow statement are core outputs, with validation so key tie-outs are checked as part of reporting — for example balance sheet balances and cash bridge to balance-sheet cash. Statement lines and waterfalls share one logic path with the dashboards and Excel packages, so you are not maintaining a separate export model.
entries.source: Reporting Logic financial statements + validation; Architecture Master

entries.title: Actual / Budget / Forecast scenarios
topics: do you support budget and forecast
entries.answer: Reporting is scenario-aware: Actual for closed periods, Budget for plan, Forecast for the rolling outlook, and a Combined view that uses Actual through the close month and Forecast thereafter. Close packages show variance columns — Actual vs Budget and Actual vs Forecast — so FP&A can review the same structure leadership already uses, not a one-scenario snapshot.
entries.source: Architecture Master scenario model; Reporting Logic Combined + period column layout

entries.title: Customize reporting per customer
topics: can each customer have different reports
keywords: can each customer have different reports
entries.answer: Yes — each customer organization has its own reporting configuration. Chart-of-accounts mapping, ARR and metric definitions, statement layouts, and which scenarios feed board and MD&A packages are set for that org. Two customers do not share one forced template; they share the same engine with different methodology configuration. Deep layout work happens at implementation, not as an ad-hoc drag-and-drop chart builder for every viewer.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper methodology-as-config; Architecture Master multi-tenancy; Reporting Architecture config rolls outputs

entries.title: Chart of accounts and methodology config
topics: do you support our chart of accounts
can you map our GL accounts
keywords: do you support our arr definition
entries.answer: Methodology is configuration the engine executes — not hardcoded one-size-fits-all logic. How you define ARR, structure management EBITDA, and map your chart of accounts into reporting lines is encoded for your organization. The engine is the same for every customer; your configuration is yours. That is how we preserve the definitions leadership already trusts instead of forcing a generic COA template.
entries.source: Technical Whitepaper, Financial Intelligence Engine — methodology is configuration

entries.title: Plan modules at a high level
entries.answer: At a high level without quoting price: Starter includes Executive Summary, ARR, Revenue, GTM, Pipeline, Risks & Validation, board export, and AI commentary. Professional adds Management P&L, Workforce, and Cash Forecast. Enterprise builds on Professional with deeper forecast packaging and enterprise commercial options — SSO and onboarding differences are discussed in sales. Exact packaging for your deal is confirmed in the order form; we do not invent dollar amounts on the call.
entries.source: GO_LIVE_GL3_PLAN_ENTITLEMENTS; frontend plan-modules.ts; STRIPE_BILLING (no public dollar amounts)

entries.title: Per-organization tenant and configuration
topics: does each customer get their own environment
keywords: does each customer get their own
entries.answer: Each customer is provisioned as its own organization tenant — separate membership, seat limits, plan entitlements, warehouse data keyed by organization, and reporting methodology configuration. You are not sharing dashboards or numbers with another company. The commercial product is multi-tenant SaaS isolation by organization, not a claim of a fully dedicated private cloud for every customer unless that is explicitly contracted.

entries.title: Connectors today vs roadmap
entries.answer: Honestly: production ingest today is versioned CSV and white-glove read-only loads into the canonical warehouse — not a claim that every Salesforce, NetSuite, or Stripe connector is generally available as a self-serve native sync. Native connectors that land in the same warehouse schema are the documented roadmap. We will not oversell connector GA; we will scope your data path for the POC and implementation.

entries.title: Board deck and MD&A packages

keywords: do you generate a board deck
entries.answer: Yes — after a period is ready for executive reporting, you can export a board PowerPoint and MD&A-style Excel / management-review packages from the same reporting layer as the live dashboards. The intent is a CFO-ready narrative package — ARR, pipeline, revenue, cash, financials — not a BI screenshot dump. AI can draft commentary bullets; it does not invent the underlying figures.

entries.title: AI commentary / Copilot
topics: does AI write the board narrative
entries.answer: AI is used for narrative assistance — variance commentary and executive summary drafting grounded in metrics the engine already calculated. It elaborates evidenced drivers; it does not compute ledger numbers or invent explanations when the data does not support them. Think evidence-backed FP&A commentary, not a chatbot that invents a story. Plan entitlements include AI commentary on the packaged tiers we ship. Verification is structural: commentary is grounded in engine outputs, humans stay in the loop for board-facing packages, and unsupported claims are declined rather than polished.

entries.title: Finance vs executive views
topics: can the board see a simpler view
entries.answer: Access is oriented for finance depth versus executive summary: finance can work with fuller drill-down into accounts and movements, while executives and board-oriented views emphasize explained summary packages. Org membership and plan entitlements gate what a signed-in user reaches inside the tenant. We describe that role orientation honestly — we do not claim a fully mature enterprise RBAC matrix with dozens of custom permission flags unless that is in your contracted scope.

entries.title: What SMPL does not do
entries.answer: We do not replace your ERP or general ledger, we do not post journals or write back to source systems, and we do not run payroll, AP, procurement, invoice generation, or tax provision. Those stay in the systems of record. SMPL reports, reconciles, explains, and packages executive output from the outcomes those systems produce.
entries.source: Architecture Master not-in-scope; Reporting Logic what this platform does NOT compute

entries.title: What is configured at implementation
entries.answer: At implementation we typically configure source data paths, chart-of-accounts and metric mapping, ARR and scenario methodology, which reports and board/MD&A packages you use, seat invites, and plan modules. Ongoing close is load → validate → finalize the period → generate executive packages — not rebuilding the model from scratch each month. Ad-hoc redesign of every chart by every user is not the product; durable methodology configuration for your org is. Calendar time depends on template-vs-one-off work and how fast access is unblocked — about a week when templates apply and access is ready; longer when discovery is heavy.

entries.answer: You can start a DIY stack — warehouse plus BI plus spreadsheet models — but the hard part is not the first dashboard. It is keeping SaaS methodology, restatements, evidence, and board-ready packages correct as systems and definitions change. Internal builds become an ongoing product your finance and data teams have to maintain. SMPL is the governed intelligence layer purpose-built for that job, so your team spends time on decisions rather than rebuilding the reporting engine every quarter.

entries.title: vs Pigment
topics: how do you compare to Pigment
keywords: how do you compare to pigment
entries.answer: Pigment is a modern planning and FP&A platform — strong at collaborative plans, scenarios, and modeling. SMPL is not trying to replace your planning tool. We are the governed financial intelligence layer above ERP, CRM, and billing: deterministic SaaS metrics, evidence-backed explanations, and executive packages that reproduce. Many customers keep planning where it is and use SMPL for trusted operating and board reporting across systems — not another place to rebuild the plan model.
entries.source: Meeting Copilot KB §5 modern FP&A complements; competitive positioning

entries.title: vs Anaplan
topics: how do you compare to Anaplan
keywords: how do you compare to anaplan
entries.answer: Anaplan is enterprise connected planning — large model workspaces for forecasting and operational plans. SMPL complements that world rather than claiming to be Anaplan. We focus on SaaS financial intelligence: ARR waterfalls, reconciled statements, evidence lineage, and board-ready narrative grounded in calculated metrics. If you already run Anaplan for planning, the question is usually whether finance still rebuilds the cross-system truth and board pack elsewhere — that is the gap we close.
entries.source: Meeting Copilot KB §5 modern FP&A complements; competitive positioning

entries.title: How accurate is the AI
entries.answer: Numbers come from the deterministic calculation engine first — same inputs and methodology produce the same outputs. AI drafts narrative over those calculated metrics; it does not invent ledger figures. Accuracy of the story depends on data completeness and your configured methodology, which is why we surface confidence signals and evidence rather than fluent guesses. If the data cannot support a claim, the platform should say so instead of sounding certain.
entries.source: Meeting Copilot KB hallucinations + determinism; company context §4

entries.title: What happens after implementation
entries.answer: After go-live the rhythm is operational, not a rebuild: load period data (CSV or white-glove path), validate, finalize the period, and generate executive dashboards plus board/MD&A packages from the same logic. Methodology and mappings stay configured for your org; you refine them when the business changes rather than reinventing reports monthly. Support and roadmap continue — we do not hand you a one-off model and disappear.
entries.source: customization-at-implementation close loop; onboarding-paths; honesty on CSV/white-glove

entries.title: Customize metrics / ARR / methodology
entries.answer: Yes — metric and methodology definitions are configuration for your organization, not a forced one-size-fits-all template. How you define ARR, map the chart of accounts, and structure management views is encoded for your tenant so two customers can differ while sharing the same engine. We configure that during implementation and can adjust as your business evolves; the product is durable methodology, not ad-hoc redesign of every chart by every user each month.

entries.title: How long until value

entries.answer: Value shows up when the first trusted close package and live dashboards replace the manual spreadsheet assemble step — same deliverables either way (dashboards, ARR, statements, board/MD&A, commentary, methodology config, validation). entries.title: What if my data is bad
topics: what if my data is bad
keywords: what if my data is bad
entries.answer: Bad or incomplete source data is normal in SaaS finance — we do not pretend otherwise. The platform surfaces confidence signals when a number is inferred or thin, and ties reported values back to source evidence so gaps are visible instead of hidden in a polished chart. Implementation focuses on validating business rules and mappings; ongoing loads include validation before you finalize a period. We help you see and fix data issues; we do not silently invent clean history.
entries.source: confidence-signal; import-validation; Meeting Copilot accuracy posture

entries.title: What if NetSuite changes
entries.answer: Source systems evolve — new accounts, custom fields, subsidiaries. Because methodology and mappings are configuration for your org, we update the mapping layer when NetSuite (or another ERP) changes rather than rewriting the product. Today ingest is versioned CSV or white-glove read-only loads into the same canonical model; when field layouts change, we adjust the load contract and re-validate before the next close. We do not claim magic zero-touch sync for every NetSuite schema change.
entries.source: data-sources-ingest honesty; connectors roadmap; methodology as config

entries.title: Custom objects support
entries.answer: Yes for the fields and objects that matter to your SaaS finance model — we map the source entities you need into the canonical warehouse during implementation rather than requiring a vanilla CRM schema. That usually covers custom Salesforce objects or fields used for bookings, renewals, or segments. Scope is the objects required for trusted metrics and reporting, landed via CSV or white-glove extract today — not an unlimited arbitrary-object marketplace claim.
entries.source: data-sources-ingest; methodology config; honesty on CSV/white-glove

entries.title: Can I export everything
entries.answer: You can export the executive and finance packages the product is built around — including board PowerPoint and MD&A-style Excel from the same logic as live dashboards — so UI and files do not drift. Drill-down and statement views are available in-product for finance. We do not promise a raw dump of every warehouse table as a self-serve bulk export of “everything”; if you need a specific extract for audit or migration, we scope that honestly rather than overselling a universal download button.
entries.source: board-deck-and-mda; dashboards-exports-same-logic; honesty boundary

entries.title: Do you replace Excel / FP&A / NetSuite
entries.answer: No on the systems of record and no on replacing your FP&A team. NetSuite (or your GL) stays the ledger; Excel stays useful for ad hoc analysis; FP&A still owns judgment, assumptions, and the story. SMPL automates the repetitive reconciliation and executive packaging layer those teams currently rebuild by hand. We complement ERP and planning tools — we do not rip out NetSuite or claim to be a full FP&A headcount substitute.
entries.source: does-not-replace-erp; compete-excel; Meeting Copilot replace questions

entries.title: Can I use my own warehouse
topics: can I use my own warehouse
do we need a data warehouse
keywords: can i use my own warehouse
do we need a data warehouse
entries.answer: A customer data warehouse is optional, not required. Existing warehouses are supported when useful — we can work from shares or exports — but SMPL is the financial intelligence layer, not another place you must park every table. Many customers start with versioned CSV or white-glove read-only loads into our model. If you already run Snowflake or similar, you still need governed SaaS methodology and explainability on top; the warehouse alone does not replace that.

entries.title: How NRR and GRR are calculated
entries.answer: NRR and GRR are native SaaS retention metrics on the ARR waterfall — not bolt-on spreadsheet formulas. They are derived from beginning ARR and the period movements (expansion, contraction, churn, and related components per your configured methodology). Exact definitions follow your org’s ARR rules configured at implementation, with drilldown to the underlying movements. We do not invent a one-off retention math that disagrees with your waterfall.
entries.source: arr-mrr-reporting; company context NRR/GRR; board ARR waterfall notes

entries.title: How forecasts and assumptions work
entries.answer: Forecasts combine historical performance with operational drivers and finance-owned assumptions inside Actual / Budget / Forecast scenarios — including Combined views that use Actual through close and Forecast thereafter. Finance remains in control: assumptions are configurable and overridable rather than locked inside a black-box model. Variance columns then compare Actual vs Budget and Actual vs Forecast so FP&A reviews the same structure leadership uses.
entries.source: Meeting Copilot forecasting; scenarios-actual-budget-forecast

entries.title: Can the board and auditors trust the numbers
topics: can the board trust the numbers
entries.answer: Trust comes from determinism, evidence, and honesty about uncertainty — not from a polished slide. The same inputs and methodology reproduce the same outputs; reported numbers tie back toward source records; confidence signals flag thin or inferred values instead of presenting them as certain. Board packages and live dashboards share one logic path. We are pursuing SOC 2 and stay transparent about certification status — we do not claim an issued SOC 2 report today.
entries.source: evidence-explainability; determinism; soc2-status honesty

entries.title: How do I trace every calculation
topics: how do I trace every calculation
keywords: how do i trace every calculation
entries.answer: Every reported number is designed to trace to the source records that produced it — invoice, opportunity, GL entry — not only an intermediate total. Explanations are generated the same way: specific drivers tied to evidence, or an explicit statement that the data does not support a sharper claim. Combined with deterministic recalculation against a period snapshot, that is how you audit “why this number” without a separate shadow spreadsheet.
entries.source: evidence-explainability; determinism; company context no black boxes

entries.title: How imports are validated
entries.answer: Loads go through validation before a period is finalized — schema and mapping checks on the versioned CSV or white-glove extract, plus business-rule validation against your configured methodology. Issues surface as data-quality and confidence problems rather than silently flowing into board numbers. Finance still owns the finalize step: we help detect and explain bad or incomplete data; we do not auto-approve a broken load into an executive package.
entries.source: close validate step (customer-safe); confidence-signal; data-sources-ingest

entries.title: AI variance and executive questions
entries.answer: Yes within governed scope: AI elaborates variance commentary and can help answer executive questions using metrics the engine already calculated and the evidence behind them. It is evidence-backed FP&A assistance — not a chatbot that invents a story when drivers are unclear. If confidence is low or evidence is missing, it should say so rather than fill the gap with fluent prose.
